title: WHY DID BIBLICAL PATRIARCHS TAKE CONCUBINES—AND WHY DID GOD ALLOW IT?
paragraphs:
WHY DID BIBLICAL PATRIARCHS TAKE CONCUBINES—AND WHY DID GOD ALLOW IT?
The Bible Never Hides the Scandal of Its Heroes. It Shows Us What Happens When Broken People Try to Accomplish God’s Promise Their Own Way—and Why Every Shattered Story Ultimately Makes Us Desperate for Jesus.
There is a question many Christians quietly carry but are sometimes afraid to ask.
If Abraham was a man of faith… why Hagar?
If Jacob was chosen by God… why Bilhah and Zilpah?

If these men were patriarchs—men whose names appear in the sacred history of redemption—why do their households sometimes look less like pictures of marital peace and more like families collapsing beneath jealousy, rivalry, wounded women, competing children, favoritism, and grief?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
Why did God allow it?
Because when you actually read the Bible instead of merely reading sanitized Bible-story versions of it, something startling happens.
The halos disappear.
Abraham struggles.
Sarah becomes desperate.
Jacob plays favorites.
Rachel burns with jealousy.
Leah aches to be loved.
Hagar runs into the wilderness.
Children inherit conflicts their parents helped create.
The Bible does not airbrush any of it.
And that may be one of the strongest evidences that we have misunderstood what Scripture is trying to show us.
The Bible is not primarily a museum displaying flawless religious heroes.
It is the story of a holy God working through profoundly flawed human beings until history arrives at the One Man who does not need His sins covered, explained, excused, or forgiven.
Jesus Christ.
So before we answer why patriarchs had concubines, we have to establish something absolutely essential:
Biblical description is not automatically biblical prescription.
The fact that Scripture tells us something happened does not mean Scripture tells us to imitate it.
Cain murdered Abel.
Abraham lied about Sarah.
Jacob deceived Isaac.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Judas betrayed Him.
Scripture records all of these things without endorsing them.
And concubinage must be read with the same care.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ—pilegesh.

In the social world reflected in the Old Testament, a concubine occupied a recognized but generally subordinate domestic position compared with a primary wife. The exact legal and social circumstances were not identical in every biblical account, so we should resist pretending that one simple modern definition explains every occurrence.
But Scripture clearly distinguishes concubines in passages such as Genesis 25:6, where Abraham’s offspring through them are distinguished from Isaac in matters of inheritance.
And here is where the Bible becomes painfully human.
In the ancient world, children meant far more than sentiment.
Children meant descendants.
Inheritance.
Household survival.
Labor.
Security.
Family continuity.
And for Abraham and Sarah, the question of descendants carried something infinitely greater:
the promise of God.
God had promised Abraham offspring.
But Sarah remained barren.
Year followed year.
Promise remained promise.
Her womb remained empty.
Imagine that pain before judging the desperation that followed it.
Every month another reminder.
Every year another disappointment.
Every promise from God apparently colliding with what her body seemed incapable of producing.
Then Sarah looked at Hagar.
And desperation whispered something that desperation still whispers today:
Maybe God needs my help.
Genesis 16 tells us that Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham so that a family might be established through her.
The Hebrew behind Sarah’s hope contains a heartbreaking wordplay around being “built up” through Hagar.
Sarah wanted a house.
A future.
A child.
Something tangible she could finally hold.
And instead of continuing to wait for the God who had promised, Abraham and Sarah attempted to produce through human strategy what God had promised through divine faithfulness.
That is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because maybe you have never taken a concubine.
But perhaps you have tried to manufacture what God told you to trust Him for.
Maybe God seemed slow, so you forced the relationship.
Maybe loneliness became unbearable, so you compromised.
Maybe money became frightening, so integrity became negotiable.
Maybe you prayed for years and eventually decided obedience was costing too much.
Maybe you knew what Scripture said—but another voice whispered:
“There has to be another way.”
That is Genesis 16.
Not merely a strange ancient sexual arrangement.
A mirror.
Human beings trying to accomplish God's purposes without waiting for God's way.
And notice what happens next.
Hagar conceives.
For one brief moment, the plan appears to work.
That may be the most dangerous part.
Disobedience sometimes produces immediate results.
The wrong relationship can temporarily soothe loneliness.
The dishonest decision can temporarily solve the financial problem.
The compromise can temporarily open the door.
The shortcut can temporarily look like an answered prayer.
Hagar became pregnant.
Problem solved?
No.
Problem multiplied.
Contempt entered the household.
Sarah became angry.
Abraham became passive.
Hagar was mistreated.
Hagar fled.
The house that was supposed to be “built” began breaking apart.
This is one of Scripture’s recurring warnings:
Just because something works does not mean God authored it.
And just because God brings redemption out of a decision does not mean He approved the decision.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because somebody reading this has been confusing God’s mercy after your compromise with God’s approval of your compromise.
They are not the same thing.
God can rescue you from a road He never told you to take.
He can forgive a sin He never commanded.
He can redeem consequences without calling the choices that created them righteous.
That is grace.
And Hagar’s story contains an astonishing picture of it.
She runs.
Pregnant.
Mistreated.
Vulnerable.
A foreign Egyptian servant caught inside someone else’s attempt to solve a spiritual problem through human means.
And God sees her.
This matters.
The narrative does not treat Hagar merely as reproductive equipment.
God meets the woman in the wilderness.
The forgotten woman is not forgotten by heaven.
The person pushed toward the margins of Abraham’s household is still visible to Abraham’s God.
Hagar responds to the God who encountered her with words associated with the astonishing confession:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i.
“You are a God who sees me.”
Think about that.
Sarah saw a solution.
Abraham saw an opportunity for an heir.
Ancient society could see a servant.
God saw Hagar.
Maybe that is why you needed this article today.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to become collateral damage in somebody else’s choices.
Someone used you.
Someone promised something and disappeared.
Someone else's selfishness changed your life.
Someone made a decision, and somehow you were the one left carrying the consequences.
People may know what happened.
God knows what it did to you.
He sees you.
Not the polished Facebook version of you.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the “I’m fine” version.
You.
And this is where the subject of concubines becomes much bigger than ancient marriage customs.
It becomes the story of what God does inside human wreckage.
Jacob’s household reinforces the lesson.
Rachel could not bear children and cried to Jacob in anguish.
Eventually her servant Bilhah entered the struggle.
Leah later gave Jacob Zilpah.
Children were born, but so were rivalry, comparison, competition, favoritism, and enormous emotional complexity.
Read those narratives slowly and you will not walk away thinking, “What a beautiful model for Christian marriage.”
You will feel the ache.
That is part of the point.
Scripture does not need to interrupt every paragraph with the sentence, “This arrangement is painful.”
The narrative shows you.
Look at the jealousy.
Look at the rivalry.
Look at the bargaining.
Look at children becoming entangled in adult wounds.
Look at women desperate to be loved.
Look at men failing to lead their households faithfully.
Look at what happens when human desire, cultural customs, reproductive desperation, power, favoritism, and sin collide.
Then go farther back.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before kings accumulated wives and concubines.
Before humanity learned how efficiently we could complicate what God created.
Return to Genesis.
God creates a man and a woman.
The man leaves father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Not one man collecting women according to wealth, power, fertility, politics, or desire.
One covenant union.
Jesus Himself reaches back to creation when teaching about marriage.
That matters enormously.
When human beings asked Jesus about difficult marital arrangements, Christ pointed beyond generations of broken human practice toward what God intended “from the beginning.”
That is how Christians should read the patriarchs.
Not by asking, “Abraham did it, so why can't I?”
But by asking:
“What was God's design before human sin distorted it?”
The patriarchs were not the standard.
God was.
And ultimately Christ is.
This also helps explain why Old Testament law can regulate broken social realities without presenting those realities as creation ideals.
God dealt with real people inside real cultures already scarred by sin.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
Restriction is not necessarily endorsement.
Tolerance within a fallen social order is not identical to declaring something morally ideal.
Jesus makes a similar distinction when discussing divorce. Moses permitted certain arrangements because of human hardness, Christ explained, but “from the beginning” it was not so.
That principle should make us very careful about building morality merely from the existence of an Old Testament practice.
God meets humanity in the wreckage.
Then He moves His people toward His holiness.
But there is another uncomfortable truth.
Concubinage was connected not merely to fertility but sometimes to wealth, status, dynasty, household expansion, and royal power.
And power has always been dangerous in the hands of sinful people.
Eventually Scripture gives us kings with multiple wives and concubines.
Solomon becomes the terrifying monument to where accumulation can lead.
The man renowned for wisdom still possessed a heart capable of wandering.
That should humble every believer.
Knowledge does not make you immune to temptation.
Ministry does not make you immune.
Bible knowledge does not make you immune.
A platform does not make you immune.
Being used by God does not make you immune.
If Abraham could stumble…
if Jacob could create terrible family dysfunction…
if David could fall…
if Solomon could wander…
then perhaps the appropriate response to biblical scandal is not arrogant judgment.
It is trembling dependence upon grace.
Because there is something frighteningly familiar about these men.
We just hide our concubines under different names.
Approval.
Pornography.
Secret messages.
Emotional affairs.
Money.
Status.
Ministry platforms.
Addictions.
Relationships we know God never told us to enter.
Private compromises we pray nobody discovers.
We create little substitutes for trust.
Things we run toward when waiting on God hurts too much.
And eventually those substitutes begin demanding payment.
That is why this article is not really about Abraham's bedroom.
It is about your heart.
And mine.
What have you brought into your life because you became tired of waiting for God?
What have you called “necessary” that Scripture calls compromise?
What have you defended simply because culture normalized it?
What have you kept because letting it go would hurt?
What is living inside your spiritual house today that God never asked you to bring inside?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because the greatest danger is not that we read Genesis and condemn Abraham.
The greatest danger is that we recognize Abraham’s impatience in ourselves and still refuse to repent.
Yet this is precisely where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
God did not abandon Abraham.
That does not mean Abraham’s failures did not matter.
It means Abraham's failures were not stronger than God's covenant faithfulness.
God continued His redemptive purpose.
Isaac came.
Jacob came.
Israel came.
Kings rose and fell.
Prophets cried out.
Generations sinned, repented, wandered, returned, failed, and waited.
Until eventually another Son appeared in the story.
Not Abraham's attempt to manufacture the promise.
Not Jacob manipulating circumstances.
Not David collapsing beneath desire.
Not Solomon drowning beneath abundance.
Jesus.
The faithful Son.
The promised Seed.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His bride but gives Himself for her.
The King who does not use His power to collect women for His pleasure but lays His life down to redeem sinners.
The Savior who encounters disgraced women without using them.
The Lord who sees the Hagar in the wilderness.
The Christ who speaks with the Samaritan woman despite her complicated relational history.
The One who receives sinners, exposes darkness, commands repentance, grants forgiveness, and creates something new.
Suddenly you understand why Scripture refuses to sanitize its heroes.
If Abraham were perfect, we might worship Abraham.
If David were spotless, we might make David our savior.
If the patriarchs were flawless, perhaps we would conclude that salvation belongs to impressive religious people.
But Scripture keeps exposing them.
And us.
Until there is only One left standing without scandal of His own.
Jesus Christ.
That is Christianity.
Not good people climbing toward God.
A holy God descending toward sinners.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace entering the scandal and rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
Not excusing Abraham.
Redeeming Abraham.
Not pretending Sarah never doubted.
Keeping the promise anyway.
Not overlooking Hagar.
Finding her in the wilderness.
Not approving everything Jacob did.
Still advancing His covenant purposes.
Not calling David's sin righteous.
Confronting him and showing mercy to the repentant.
This is why grace is so offensive to pride.
Grace means your worst chapter can be real without becoming your final chapter.
But grace never says sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
At Calvary, Jesus was not demonstrating that sin was insignificant.
He was demonstrating how terrible sin truly is—and how astonishingly far divine love would go to save sinners.
The cross simultaneously destroys our excuses and destroys our despair.
You cannot look at Calvary and say sin doesn't matter.
And you cannot look at Calvary and say repentant sinners cannot be forgiven.
Both lies die there.
Maybe your story contains scandal.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your marriage carries wounds you helped create.
Maybe your children have suffered because of decisions you regret.
Maybe sexual sin has followed you for years.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe you tried to force God's timing and created consequences you cannot undo.
Maybe you are reading about Abraham and realizing that underneath the ancient clothing, tents, servants, and inheritance customs is something terrifyingly familiar:
a human being who believed God…
and still had moments when waiting became unbearable.
Listen carefully.
Your failure does not become righteous simply because a patriarch also failed.
But neither must failure become your final identity when Jesus Christ offers forgiveness to those who repent and believe.
Repentance means we stop renaming darkness.
We stop saying, “Everybody does it.”
We stop saying, “That's just how culture works.”
We stop saying, “God understands,” when what we really mean is, “I don't want to surrender this.”
God does understand.
More deeply than you know.
And because He understands, He calls you out of the thing destroying you.
Grace does not merely comfort you inside chains.
Grace breaks chains.
Jesus does not merely rewrite your reputation.
He transforms your heart.
That is the difference between cheap religious reassurance and the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say:
“You're okay. Keep going.”
It says:
“You are loved. Now come home.”
Talk to Christ.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Receive His mercy.
Not because typing words beneath a Facebook post saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops pretending.
And maybe your comment will give another wounded believer enough courage to stop hiding too.
Let someone else know they are not the only believer struggling to trust God in the waiting.
There is no trophy for pretending to be strong.
There is grace for people who know they need Christ.
Not because every paragraph is comfortable, but because someday impatience may whisper that compromise is easier than obedience.
Come back and remember Hagar.
Come back and remember Abraham.
Come back and remember Sarah.
Come back and remember:
God does not need your sin to accomplish His promise.
Someone else may be living inside the consequences of a shortcut they deeply regret.
Someone may believe their scandal has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Let this reach them.
And yes—even send it to the skeptical friend who thinks the Bible hides the failures of its heroes.
It doesn't.
That is part of its power.

At Gospel Warrior, we do not want to build a community that survives on inspirational slogans while avoiding difficult Scripture. We want believers who can open the Bible, encounter uncomfortable passages, understand them in context, bow before Jesus Christ, repent when the Word exposes them, and grow into mature disciples.
Not because paying money earns favor with God.
It absolutely does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.

Your support helps us keep putting Scripture-centered material in front of believers, struggling Christians, seekers, families, and people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Biblical nourishment.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
Growing deeper in Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker with uncomfortable questions.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity cannot survive honest examination.
But before you leave, remember the question we started with.
Why did biblical patriarchs take concubines?

Because they lived in a fallen world where concubinage existed within the social realities of their cultures; because questions of fertility, descendants, inheritance, household continuity, status, and power mattered enormously; and sometimes, as Genesis painfully demonstrates, because even people of genuine faith made profoundly human decisions shaped by fear, impatience, desire, cultural expectations, and attempts to secure with their own hands what they should have entrusted to God.
God's willingness to work through those broken stories does not transform every human decision within them into His ideal.
Instead, their failures make us long for something better.
Someone better.
Abraham could not carry the weight of being humanity's savior.
Jacob could not.
Judah could not.
Moses could not.
David could not.
Solomon could not.
You cannot.
I cannot.
There is only Jesus.
And perhaps that is why the Bible lets the scandal remain on the page.
Because God was never trying to convince us that His people were flawless.
He was showing us that His grace is relentless.
The genealogy keeps moving.
The promise keeps breathing.
Grace keeps pursuing.
Until Bethlehem.
Until a cross.
Until an empty tomb.
Until sinners like us discover that God has been writing redemption through broken human history all along.
So stop trying to hide the chapter Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Bring Him the impatience.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the consequences.
Bring Him the wilderness.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish could be ripped out of the book.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Christ.
Because the same Bible that refuses to hide Abraham's household also refuses to end humanity's story there.
And neither does your story have to end at your worst chapter.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but when surrendered to Jesus, it does not get the authority to decide where your story ends.
